title: Meet the 13 people proposed as Nepal’s new ambassadors - Onlinekhabar English
description: Meet the 13 people proposed as Nepal’s new ambassadors  Onlinekhabar English
publisher.title: Onlinekhabar English
full_article:
Kathmandu, September 18

The government has recommended 13 individuals for appointment as Nepal’s ambassadors to different countries, including India, China, the United States and the United Kingdom.

A Cabinet meeting held on Friday recommended the names of individuals with backgrounds in diplomacy, academia, security, development, business, public policy and other fields.

The recommended names will now be sent to the Parliamentary Hearing Committee. Following parliamentary hearings, the government will seek agrément from the respective countries. Once agrément is received, the President will formally appoint the nominees as ambassadors.

Here is a look at the backgrounds of the 13 proposed ambassadors.

1. Dr Nischal Nath Pandey — India

Dr Nischal Nath Pandey is an academic and foreign policy expert who currently serves as director of the Centre for South Asian Studies (CSAS).

He previously served as executive director of the Institute of Foreign Affairs under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1998 to 2006 and as an adviser to the National Planning Commission on tourism and civil aviation from 1996 to 1997.

Pandey also served as an expert with Nepal’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 2016 and as a member of a high-level foreign policy task force formed by the government in 2017.

He holds a PhD in political science and an LLB from Tribhuvan University. He has also served as an honorary associate professor at the National Institute of Advanced Studies in Bengaluru and as a non-resident senior fellow at the Institute of South Asian Studies at the National University of Singapore.

Pandey has completed visiting fellowships at Germany’s SWP in Berlin and the University of Hull in the UK. He has also served on the board of the Regional Centre for Strategic Studies in Colombo.

He has authored three books published by SAGE and Manohar Publishers, along with numerous edited works on Nepal’s foreign policy and regional cooperation. In 2015, he completed the South Asia Leadership Executive Program at Harvard Kennedy School.

2. Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma — China

Dr Kalyan Raj Sharma is a Nepal-China affairs expert, sinologist and economist with more than two decades of experience in academia, institutional governance and bilateral policy cooperation.

He holds a PhD in economics from Fudan University, where his research focused on foreign direct investment, trade and tourism financing.

Sharma is currently chairman of the Fudan University Alumni Association Nepal, the Nepal-China Friendship Forum and the Council of Sinologists-Nepal. He also serves as a visiting scholar at Kathmandu University School of Management, where he developed and teaches a course on doing business in China.

He is managing director of Adventure Outdoor Excursion and has been involved in promoting Himalayan and cross-border tourism. He also serves as an independent board director at Apex Funds and several hydropower and energy companies.

For his contribution to Nepal-China relations, Sharma received the Nepal Bhushan from the President of Nepal in 2016 and the Silk Road Friendship Award in 2021.

3. Chiran Jung Thapa — United States

Chiran Jung Thapa is a national security and international affairs expert with more than two decades of experience in security policy, crisis management and diplomacy.

He holds a master’s degree in international affairs from Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, which he completed on a full academic scholarship, and a bachelor’s degree in international relations from SUNY Geneseo.

Since 2017, Thapa has served as Oxfam’s regional security adviser for Asia, where he has led risk and crisis management work across 15 countries.

Previously, he worked as regional security and justice adviser for Asia at Saferworld from 2013 to 2016 and as an adviser on security sector and civil-military relations at The Asia Foundation from 2010 to 2013.

During his career, he has advised Nepal’s Ministry of Defence, National Security Council, Nepal Army and Nepal Police. He also developed the Nepal Army’s first civil-military relations course.

Earlier, he worked with the permanent missions of Singapore and Nepal to the United Nations in New York.

Thapa completed Harvard Kennedy School’s Leadership in Homeland Security programme and has worked in Nepal, the United States, the United Kingdom and several countries in South and Southeast Asia.

4. Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana — United Kingdom

Former Chief of Army Staff Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana has more than four decades of experience in the Nepal Army and served as chief of army staff from 2012 to 2015.

During his tenure, he oversaw the integration of former Maoist combatants into the Nepal Army under the Comprehensive Peace Agreement. He also led the army during Nepal’s transition to a federal democratic republic.

Rana was involved in implementing the army’s 10-year long-term plan and Military Doctrine 2013.

Following the 2015 earthquake, he led the Nepal Army’s disaster response operation, Operation Sankat Mochan, and coordinated the involvement of 18 foreign military teams in relief efforts.

He previously served as chief of staff, director general of the Directorate General of Military Operations and commander of Nepal’s UNIFIL battalion in southern Lebanon.

Rana holds a master’s degree in defence and strategic studies from Quaid-i-Azam University in Pakistan and a bachelor’s degree in history and political science from Tribhuvan University. He is also a graduate of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the US Army Command and General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth and Pakistan’s National Defence University.

5. Jigyan Kumar Thapa — Japan

Jigyan Kumar Thapa has more than two decades of experience working to strengthen Nepal-Japan relations.

He holds a master’s degree in international relations and law from Yokohama National University and a bachelor’s degree in international cooperation from Shumei University.

Since 2009, he has worked at the Kanagawa International Foundation as an expert on international cooperation, public policy and multicultural affairs.

Since 2005, he has also coordinated high-level Nepal-Japan bilateral programmes, facilitating visits and exchanges involving presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers of both countries.

Thapa organised the Nepal-Japan Business Dialogue during the Nepali president’s official visit to Japan in 2026.

He has worked closely with JICA, UNICEF and Japanese local governments on international cooperation and migration governance initiatives. He has also served as an adviser to the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Nepal, former general secretary of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan and former president of the Nepali Students Association in Japan.

He has taught as an associate professor at several Japanese universities and is proficient in Japanese, having passed JLPT Level 1.

6. Suresh Kumar Karn — Israel

Suresh Kumar Karn is a senior professional with more than 30 years of experience in information technology, banking and economic policy.

While serving as chief information and marketing officer at Kumari Bank from 2003 to 2015, he developed and launched Kumari Mobile Cash, described as Nepal’s first mobile wallet.

He later served as chief operating officer of Nepal Bank from 2015 to 2019, where he led the bank’s transition to an integrated core banking system.

Since 2024, Karn has chaired Kumo Labs, a Japanese technology investment established under Nepal’s Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act.

He has also served two consecutive terms as president of the Computer Association of Nepal Federation and was a member of Nepal’s IT Council and the High-Level Commission for Information Technology.

Karn contributed to drafting Nepal’s first national IT policy in 2000. He holds an MBA in international trade, investment and infrastructure economics from Beijing Normal University’s Belt and Road School.

He began his career as an inspector in the Nepal Police and has also received the National ICT Excellence Award.

7. Prapti Sherchan — Spain

Prapti Sherchan is an international development and partnership professional with 15 years of experience across South Asia, Southeast Asia and Africa.

She has worked at the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, since 2015 and currently serves as an operations officer for gender solutions and impact.

She has led IFC India’s gender country programme and previously served as the Asia lead for IFC’s women’s insurance programme, helping expand inclusive finance partnerships across Asia and Africa.

The programme has covered more than 1.3 million women and contributed to the creation of 9,500 jobs, according to the profile provided by the government.

Sherchan has also led multi-country research initiatives involving Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka and a 10-country regional study with the ASEAN Insurance Council.

She holds an MBA in sustainable international development from Brandeis University’s Heller School and a bachelor’s degree in sociology from the National University of Singapore.

She has represented IFC at high-level international forums, including the World Bank-IMF Spring Meetings. She is also co-chair of the US board of Women Lead Nepal and co-founder of the IFC Millennial+ Resource Group.

8. Saru Joshi — Germany

Saru Joshi is a senior policy expert with more than 25 years of experience in foreign employment governance, gender equality and international cooperation.

She has contributed to the development of Nepal’s migration framework, including the Foreign Employment Act 2007, Foreign Employment Rules 2008 and Foreign Employment Policy 2012.

Joshi worked at UN Women for a decade, serving as regional programme manager for South Asia and head of labour diplomacy from 2002 to 2012.

She later served as a programme specialist and head of the Women’s Economic Empowerment Unit at UN Women Nepal, followed by a role as strategic partnership specialist.

Since 2018, she has worked as an independent senior policy and international relations consultant. Her work has included advising UN Women, the World Bank and the Global Forum on Migration and Development.

She has represented Nepal at international forums including COP28.

Since 2024, Joshi has served on the executive board of the Nepal Policy Institute and has been involved in advocacy for voting rights for Nepali migrant workers.

She holds master’s degrees in women and development from the Institute of Social Studies in The Hague and political science from Tribhuvan University. She is also the author of the book Euta Sinko Bhachera Herdā and has published more than 60 articles on foreign employment and gender issues.

9. Dr Padmakshi Rana — Oman

Dr Padmakshi Rana is a development and entrepreneurship professional with more than 15 years of experience in sustainable development, inclusive innovation and international cooperation across Nepal, Asia and Europe.

Since 2022, she has served as executive director and co-founder of Impact Hub Kathmandu, representing Nepal within the Impact Hub Global Association and its Asia-Pacific regional network.

She has developed partnerships with organisations including UK Aid/FCDO, the European Union, UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCAP, the World Bank and the Royal Academy of Engineering.

Rana holds a PhD in corporate social responsibility in food production from the University of Cambridge’s Institute for Manufacturing. She also holds an MPhil in environment, society and development from Cambridge and an MBA from Webster University Thailand.

Before joining Impact Hub, she held research and teaching positions at Cambridge and co-founded a sustainability innovation consultancy in Singapore.

Her research has focused on sustainable business models in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region and post-disaster tourism recovery.

10. Chudamani Kharel — Malaysia

Chudamani Kharel has an academic background in humanities, English, political science and law and has worked in education and public administration.

He holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in English, a master’s degree in political science and an LLB from Tribhuvan University.

Kharel is currently general secretary of the Nepal Yoga Sports Association. He previously served as general secretary of the Nepal Skating and Skateboarding Association and as member-secretary of the 7th National Games subcommittee under the National Sports Council.

His academic career includes several years as a lecturer in English at Cosmos College and John Bauer College.

11. Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha — South Korea

Prof Dr Sangam Shrestha is an academic and global policy expert with more than 25 years of experience in international cooperation, climate resilience and water-security diplomacy.

He is currently a professor at the School of Engineering and Technology at the Asian Institute of Technology in Thailand and a former dean of the school. He is also founding co-director of the Global Water and Sanitation Center.

Shrestha has worked with the Asian Development Bank, World Bank, Gates Foundation, UN agencies, European Union, FAO and UNESCO on international grants and cooperation.

He has worked with governments and diplomatic missions in more than 30 countries.

He holds a PhD in integrated river basin management from Yamanashi University in Japan and has published more than 200 research papers.

He has also served as a visiting professor at Beijing Normal University and the National University of Laos and has supervised more than 20 PhD students and over 150 postgraduate students across Asia.

12. Dr Manchala Jha — Sri Lanka

Dr Manchala Jha is a governance and public policy expert who served as a commissioner at Nepal’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission from 2015 to 2019.

During her tenure, she represented the commission at international transitional justice forums and presented Nepal’s experience with truth, justice and reconciliation in Sri Lanka.

She is an associate professor at Tribhuvan University and taught in its master’s programme on governance and corruption control from 2021 to 2024.

Jha holds a PhD in Hindi literature from B.R. Ambedkar University in India and master’s degrees in political science, with a specialisation in foreign policy and diplomacy, and Hindi literature from Tribhuvan University.

She has also served as an invited expert on Nepal’s national implementation and monitoring committee for the United Nations Istanbul Programme of Action.

Jha has provided training to government and civil society stakeholders on women, peace and security under UN Security Council resolutions 1325 and 1820.

She has worked as an election observer and media analyst on Nepali politics and governance and is proficient in Nepali, Hindi, English and Maithili.

13. Giribahadur Sunar — Saudi Arabia

Giribahadur Sunar is a sociologist and development professional with more than 25 years of experience in international development, policy advice and multi-stakeholder governance.

His areas of expertise include social safeguards, gender equality and social inclusion, community-based climate adaptation and grievance redress mechanisms.

He has applied this expertise to major infrastructure and water-sector programmes supported by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank.

Sunar is pursuing a PhD in sociology at Tribhuvan University and completed an MPhil in 2019.

He is the author of Empowering Women Through Self-Defense , published by Scholars Press in Germany, and has written more than 100 policy articles for Nepali newspapers including The Himalayan Times , The Annapurna Express and Republica .

He also serves as secretary of Social, Environment and Rural Development Nepal (SERD-Nepal) and has appeared as a public diplomacy commentator on national television.

title: In a Nepal town, flood survivors find little trace of former lives - 1470 & 100.3 WMBD
description: In a Nepal town, flood survivors find little trace of former lives  1470 & 100.3 WMBD

full_article:
By Adnan Abidi, Tyrone Siu and Sahana Bajracharya

BETRAWATI, Nepal/DEVIGHAT, Nepal, Sept 18 (Reuters) – Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing about Nepal’s devastating floods, hoping that her beloved grandmother was one of those who survived.

She headed for the family’s two-storey house in the small town of Betrawati.

But there was no house, and no Betrawati.

Those who escaped ​last month’s disaster, when a torrent of mud and rocks swept across the Nepal-China border area, have been returning to see ‌what they can recover. In some cases, all they have found is a flat expanse of grey silt.

Standing on the hardened mud, the 23-year-old Magar wondered whether her grandmother, who could barely walk, was beneath the ground. “Aama” — mother, in Nepalese — was last seen resting on her bed.

“If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?” said Magar.

Each day, scores of survivors sheltering in clusters of tents on a hillside above the site of Betrawati walk the half a kilometre (500 yards) to wander across ‌the ​wasteland that was once their town, searching for traces of homes, shops and loved ones swallowed ⁠by the floods.

There are 5,130 people still reported ⁠missing on the Nepal side of the border after the flood caused by a glacial collapse that swept down the mountains, killing at least 1,386 people. The authorities continue to search for survivors, but it has been days since anyone has been found alive.

A TRAIL OF PANIC

The highway linking Bidur to Betrawati has been replaced by a thick layer of mud deposited by the flood-swollen river.

Reaching Betrawati ​now requires climbing a steep hillside, traversing a narrow ridge and then descending into what had been a bustling settlement.

Along the way lie abandoned shoes and slippers, silent evidence of the panic that unfolded as people scrambled to escape the torrent of water, mud and rock. A deserted ⁠school building stands half-buried in debris. Further up the trail, children’s shoes, school ties, ⁠and backpacks are scattered across the mud.

The floodwaters surged downstream with such force that they slammed into the ​base of a hill before rebounding across the valley, sweeping away everything in their path.

Betrawati residents said warnings about the approaching flood began circulating minutes ​before it arrived, as friends and relatives upstream phoned to alert them. But few grasped the speed or ‌scale of what was coming.

Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled receiving a call from a friend, telling her: “Run! Run!”

“I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me,” she said.

In Devighat, downstream, partial shells of houses still stand. Residents have been salvaging what belongings they can, though many say they will have no reason to return again.

Madhav Ghimire, 42, carries the keys to the six-room ⁠house he shared with Ambika Aryal, 38, but the landscape has changed so dramatically that they can no longer identify where it stood.

“Though I lost everything, I have still carried the keys of my home. It gives me a sense that I have everything,” he said.

LOST EVERYTHING

For many families ⁠in the region, it was not the first disaster ‌they had endured. Nearly 9,000 people were killed in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake.

Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana’s ⁠older sister, said the earthquake had brought hardship and loss, but families had at least been able ​to salvage ‌belongings and rebuild on their land. This time, the two houses she owned with her husband had ​been swept away ⁠and their farmland buried under debris.

“This time, we have lost everything,” she said.

Shanti Dangol, 61, stood on a single broken tile, the only visible trace of her home, holding a photograph of the three-storey lodge that once stood there.

She described Betrawati as a once-thriving town that catered to pilgrims and trekkers and had grown more prosperous in recent years as families built larger homes, rented rooms and invested in their children’s education.

“Economically, people here had started doing well. Now, nothing remains,” she said.

(Photography and reporting by Adnan Abidi and Tyrone Siu; Addtional reporting by Sahana Bajracharya and Thomas Suen; Writing by ​Aftab Ahmed; Editing by Rosalba O’Brien)

full_article:
A Singaporean climber died on Mount Manaslu in Nepal after taking unwell during an acclimatisation rotation, the expedition organiser said.

Lau Wee Seng, 50, died on 17 September at an altitude of about 6,000m, according to Nepalese media and his expedition organiser.

"He passed away this morning. Arrangements have been made to airlift his body," Pemba Sherpa of 8K Expeditions said on Thursday.

Lau reached Camp II on 16 September and stayed overnight before beginning his descent the following morning, according to Lakpa Sherpa, founder of 8K Expeditions. During the descent, he stopped to rest and lost his pulse within a minute, Mr Lakpa told The Straits Times.

Lau is the second climber, and first foreigner, to die on Manaslu this season. Tashi Sherpa, a 20-year-old Nepali porter, was found dead in a tent at the mountain's base camp earlier this month. Police said he had gone to sleep in a tent containing a generator without informing others. An investigation into the circumstances of his death was reported to be underway.

Meanwhile, expedition operators are working to open the route towards the Manaslu summit. An avalanche struck the slope above Camp III on 16 September, disrupting rope-fixing work, although members of the rope-fixing team were reported to be safe.

At least 480 foreign climbers have obtained permits to attempt Manaslu this autumn, with Nepal's tourism dDepartment collecting $1.44m in royalties.

The autumn season is generally less popular with climbers than spring because of colder and shorter days, snowier conditions, and a narrower window for summit attempts.

title: Flood-damaged Nepal wants help from the global climate Loss and Damage Fund – but it’s waiting, along with 118 other countries - theconversation.com
description: Flood-damaged Nepal wants help from the global climate Loss and Damage Fund – but it’s waiting, along with 118 other countries  theconversation.com
publisher.title: theconversation.com
full_article:
As it faces the enormous task of rebuilding from a deadly flood that tore through communities in the Himalayas, Nepal is seeking compensation from the international Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage – meaning from countries that are major contributors to climate change, which it blames for the disaster.

Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said it was not merely a request for aid or charity but a demand for justice and “legal and moral liability.”

“Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create,” Khanal told the Kathmandu Post. “The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.”

The New York Times compiled images from mountaineers and maps showing how the glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, 2026.

Nepal’s US$20 million request is small compared to the billions of dollars in damage, but it is an important test of the Loss and Damage Fund’s credibility. So far the fund, created during the U.N. climate conference in 2022 to respond to the impacts of climate change in developing countries, contains a fraction of the money major greenhouse gas emitters pledged to contribute, and it has paid out nothing despite requests from at least 119 nations.

Climate change is raising the risk

It is scientifically well established that global temperatures are rising and fueling ice melt and more extreme climate and weather conditions around the world.

Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, largely from burning fossil fuels, have pushed global temperatures so high that sea levels are rising, and shrinking glaciers and thawing permafrost are leaving mountainsides less stable. A September 2026 U.N. Environment Program report determined that it is now inevitable that the planet will warm by at least 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to temperatures before the Industrial Revolution. Communities will have to adapt to increasing hazards.

The world committed under the Paris climate agreement to try to limit warming to 1.5 C in an attempt to avoid the worst effects of climate change. But it is not on track, and many countries are paying the price.

Is the fund just words?

At least 119 countries have submitted requests for money from the Loss and Damage Fund to help them respond to disasters or adapt to climate change.

About 93% of the requests as of June 2026 involved extreme events such as floods. Over three-quarters included slow-onset events, such as requests for help building the infrastructure, including sea walls, and the capabilities to adapt to sea-level rise.

Together, the requests totaled $2.8 billion – about 10 times the amount of money that had actually reached the fund.

Wealthy countries have so far pledged to give about $820 million to the Loss and Damage Fund, but they have delivered only about a third of that – $250 million to $300 million. The U.S. withdrew its support for the fund in 2025.

The fund’s board, meanwhile, has yet to disburse money for any of the requests. At the most recent board meeting in June 2026, officials considered four requests for funding, but none were approved.

The board has a responsibility to ensure that the money will be used appropriately. But one analysis of comments countries made while negotiating the creation of the fund and decisions of the fund board suggested that the slowness of both the disbursals and the setting up of the fund had been deliberate – a practical evasion of a responsibility agreed to on paper.

The board is scheduled to meet next in December 2026. Eight of the 26 board members formally requested an emergency meeting to respond to the disaster in Nepal quickly. The co-chairs of the board acknowledged the request, but how the board might respond was unclear.

Nepal needs billions for recovery

Nepal is asking for about $20 million from the fund. However, the country’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, estimated that the country would need US$4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild from the flood damage – nearly a tenth of its national economy.

Nepal lost over 10% of its hydropower capacity when a glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, causing the landslide and flood. Mud, water and rock inundated several riverside communities near the border with China, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing. The flood also broke through several hydropower dams in the Bhote Koshi river basin.

The flood buried several riverside communities in mud and rock and damaged more than a dozen hydropower dams, knocking out about a tenth of Nepal’s power production. Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images

In Nepal, many of the risks come from melting glaciers. The Himalayas and neighboring Hindu Kush mountains together contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice, but studies show they have been losing that ice fast as temperatures rise, with the loss rate doubling since 2000. When glaciers retreat, the result can create glacial lakes prone to outburst floods and unstable slopes prone to landslides like Nepal experienced.

Nepal is receiving aid directly from other countries, but it wants support from the Loss and Damage Fund in part because of what that would represent.

The symbolism of the Loss and Damage Fund

In many ways, the fund is symbolic, and that symbolism is important.

Vulnerable countries fought through years of international climate talks to establish a principle of climate compensation and distinguish it from charity. Even if the amount that the fund disburses to Nepal is relatively small, it would represent compensation for harm caused by climate change.

Countries are often willing to provide humanitarian assistance, but they are resistant to providing funding labeled “loss and damage,” unwilling to assume responsibility – and potentially liability – for climate change.

People in the town of Devighat try to clean a home that was covered by the landslide’s debris. Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images

The decision establishing the fund is very clear that contributions are voluntary and the act of contributing should not be interpreted as an acknowledgment of liability. Climate-vulnerable countries consented to that language in the hope that it would bring in much-needed help.

If the fund acts promptly and pragmatically on that shared responsibility, global efforts to establish liability for climate change through international tribunals and courts could ease.

Speed matters

To be effective, the Loss and Damage Fund needs to be more agile and responsive to the needs of the most climate-vulnerable countries. During negotiations to set up the fund, one negotiator emphasized the need for resources to be accessible within 24 to 48 hours of a climate disaster.

A coalition of experienced adaptation and disaster response organizations has argued that the fund should prioritize effective existing local and national programs and low-cost and low-risk projects. These include community-based resilience and recovery with local volunteers, health centers and cash transfers to flood-affected households.

France 24 used amateur video from along the flood’s path to reconstruct the damage.

From response to anticipation

The Loss and Damage Fund could also use its symbolic and modest financial position to nudge the broader humanitarian, development and climate finance ecosystem toward what’s known as anticipatory action.

Anticipatory action involves moving resources into at-risk places before the disaster hits. It has been proven to speed up the response and recovery.

Emphasizing this approach could also lead to better forecasting, early warnings and planning that takes climate change into account to protect people in vulnerable regions around the world.

title: Nepal floods: ‘Apocalyptic’ destruction signals wider climate threat across Himalayas - UN News
description: Nepal floods: ‘Apocalyptic’ destruction signals wider climate threat across Himalayas  UN News
publisher.title: UN News
full_article:
The warning comes from Sara Netzer, regional director with UN field operations office UNOPS, which provides infrastructure, procurement and project management services across the world.

Fresh from Nepal, she updated journalists in Geneva on the extent of the destruction, how UNOPS and partners have been supporting the response, and the difficulties of building back after devastation.

“As we think about reconstruction, normally two to three weeks after a disaster, we would start to see communities rebuilding,” she said, speaking from Bangkok. “But that can’t be the case in these communities in Nepal.”

Communities ‘completely obliterated’

The flash floods and landslides – triggered by a glacier collapse in late August – killed more than 1,200 people. Homes were moved wholesale up to 150 metres from where they once stood.

Ms. Netzer described visiting some of the hardest hit areas, including one community of some 400 homes, and 1,200 people, where “everything was completely obliterated” by a wall of water and mud.

“It looks like an apocalypse,” she stressed, adding that the debris left behind is between five and eight metres deep.

Death, destruction and debris

“The debris has everything you can imagine you can see in it,” she continued. “Eyeglasses, schoolbooks, shoes, blankets and, sadly, also likely the remains of loved ones as well.”

Ms. Netzer said that displaced people are now living in what the Nepali government calls holding centres. The UNOPS team visited some of these locations, where adequate water and sanitation are urgent needs.

As many of the displaced are essentially living in schools which the authorities would like to reopen, emergency temporary shelter is also an urgent requirement.

“This is particularly important for children who have experienced this tremendous trauma of seeing loved ones washed away in front of their eyes,” she said.

“Many of them now do not have parents, and they’re also in these holding centres, so as soon as they can return to some sense of normalcy and return to school, that would be beneficial for them.”

Building back on “Jell-O”

Meanwhile, prospects for reconstruction appear less optimistic because “the river has completely changed its course, so it’s not even clear where it is safe for these communities to rebuild and to return”, the UNOPS official continued.

She described the land underfoot as uneven and “very much like Jell-O”, saying it “hasn't even settled yet to begin to think about rebuilding and reconstruction.”

UNOPS has mobilized funding to support urgent engineering assessments, risk mapping of infrastructure and bridge safety analysis.

The issue of access across waterways is crucial as only one of the 40 bridges in the area is still standing, leaving communities completely cut off. This has also affected humanitarian operations, with the World Food Programme (WFP) having to rely on helicopters to deliver lifesaving aid.

“Overall, it's a crisis with tremendous human costs, tremendous costs in terms of infrastructure,” she said.

In this recent interview, Ms. Netzer explains how the overall destruction is unlike anything she saw after the 2015 earthquake in NepaL.

Fears of repetition

Ms. Netzer recalled that some of the affected communities had already been displaced by the disastrous earthquake a decade ago. People who spoke to the UNOPS team expressed concern over rebuilding and the psychological impacts they face.

These people “have lost everything”, she said, including loved ones, some of whom were breadwinners in the family. Many relatives are also still missing.

“I think what we’re seeing in Nepal is something that could be repeated across the Himalayas as we look at climate change going forward,” she said.

“It’s a crisis that maybe today is affecting Nepal but has the likelihood of affecting another community or another country going forward.”

title: After the flood, Nepal braces for disease outbreaks - gavi.org
description: After the flood, Nepal braces for disease outbreaks  gavi.org
publisher.title: gavi.org
full_article:
At a glance The collapse of a glacier triggered a flood that has killed more than 1,500 people in Nepal, leaving 6,150 people still unaccounted for. An estimated 32,000 people have been displaced, with more than 80,000 in need of aid.

While early response efforts have focused on search-and-rescue, health leaders say that efforts to control the spread of infectious disease in the flood zone have been underway since the beginning. Vaccination campaigns are ongoing.

Researchers emphasise that the glacier’s collapse is a climate change-linked event. As global temperatures continue to rise, it’s unlikely to be the last disaster of its kind.

The morning of August 26 was fine and clear until suddenly it wasn’t, recalls Bishal Khadka, a bank branch manager in Timmure, Rasuwa, in Nepal’s Bagmati Province. He had just arrived at the office and was settling in when his chair lurched beneath him. He thought it was an earthquake, and dashed out of doors.

A security guard working in the same building ran out calling to him: “Sir, run fast, it’s not an earthquake. Something very huge – a mass – it’s coming to us from the sky from China’s side.”

The mass was sludgy water, charged up with solid debris; a flood was sweeping away everything in its path. Khadka said he saw a muddied car fly out of nowhere and land in the road.

Khadka and the guard ran uphill, through thorny scrub. When they paused to look back they saw Timmure had been washed away.

A “Himalayan Tsunami”

Timmure is the first village in Nepal after crossing the China border. The disastrous flash flood of 26 August is believed to have been the result of a glacier collapse on Mount Langtang Lirung, which is situated on the Nepal-China Border.

Locals said the flood covered the 80-kilometre distance from Rasuwagadhi to Devighat Bazaar in a mere 25 minutes.

More than 1,500 people have been reported killed, with 6,150 people still unaccounted for in Nepal, according to government estimates.

A cholera vaccination campaign is being launched to prevent its spread in flood-affected areas. Credit: Public Health Office Rasuwa

At the time of writing, 13,583 people had been rescued and 3,240 people were taking shelter in 1 of 17 holding centres. Five districts, 15 municipalities and 49 wards have been directly affected, with an estimated population of 32,000 facing displacement. According to the United Nations Development Programme, more than 84,000 people are in need of aid.

Experts here in Nepal have described the catastrophe as the “Himalayan Tsunami”, and have clearly identified it as a climate change-linked event. As global temperatures rise, glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya mountain range – which spans Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan – have lost ice 65% faster between 2011 and 2020 than during the previous decade. Nepal alone has lost close to one third of its ice volume in roughly three decades, the United Nations said in 2023.

The greatest irony is that Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, which is thought to be the most important contributor for global warming. That means the people of Nepal, and people from elsewhere in the Himalayas, are paying the price for a problem created elsewhere. The total economic losses for Nepal subsequent to the flood are estimated at US$ 2.70 billion. Those losses aren’t static. The damage sustained by no fewer than 13 hydropower facilities and projects, for instance, will jeopardise Nepal’s energy strategy, which will, in turn, have bearing on the national budget and consequently on health systems in general.

Round two: a wave of disease

The second-round dangers are still gathering speed.

The floodwaters travelled at a pace of approximately 180 km/h per hour, sweeping away houses, people, livestock, food grains and other belongings. All that biological debris has now started to decompose.

Dr Dipendra Pandey, a senior orthopaedic surgeon who recently visited the epicentre of the disaster in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts shared his experience with VaccinesWork . “I had actually visited those districts to provide aid in trauma care,” he said, “but what I found was that almost all parts of the river bank is smelling very bad with dead bodies. Water sources supplying the living [people] are almost all contaminated. Displaced people lack even the basic facilities to maintain their health hygiene. So I fear there might be infectious disease outbreak in those areas.”

To complicate matters further, health service infrastructure has been severely affected in the disaster-hit areas, with four health posts fully damaged, at least one hospital partially damaged and access to two further hospitals compromised. Many of the health workers now rushing to the aid of the displaced are victims of the disaster themselves.

Unnati Maharjan, Public Health Officer at Rasuwa District, highlighted some emerging public health issues at the affected areas. Thousands of people have sudden lylost their homes, which means they are either in holding centres prepared by government, gumbas (sacred Buddhist monastery compounds) or in their relatives’ houses. The upshot is crowding. Diarrhoeal illness, viral respiratory conditions and fungal infections are far more likely to spread quickly under these conditions, and are already doing so.

According to Maharjan, children living at a holding centres on the grounds of Nilakantha Higher Secondary School in Rasuwa developed fevers and rashes, which rapidly spread among them. Suspected to have measles, infected children were kept at isolation and samples from four children were sent to Kathmandu for laboratory testing. Luckily, it turned to be a different, and less life-threatening viral illness.

A health worker checks the health status of a child staying in a camp at Nilkantha Secondary School in Rasuwa after showing measles-like symptoms. Credit: Public Health Office Rasuwa

Meanwhile, many in the geriatric and chronically ill population have lost access to their regular medication along with their homes. Health workers are struggling to get hold of the right prescription medicines in time.

And for many, financial losses have direct health impacts. Raj Kumar Dangol, who was scheduled to donate his kidney to his wife next month, had kept 2.5 million Nepali rupees at his home earmarked for the surgery. All that money has been lost. He became so hopeless that he started crying in an appeal video. The video went viral on various social media platforms. Afterwards, a few businessman pledged him to help him fund his wife’s renal transplant.

Have you read? Outbreaks signal new delays for Nepal’s mission to eliminate measles

How a 'nightmare' cholera outbreak brought Nepali hospitals to the brink

Sandbags against the tide

In the initial days, the major focus of the government was in rescuing the survivors and getting the injured treated in a timely manner.

Since all motorable roads were swept away by flood, rescue was possible only with the helicopters in the difficult geographical terrain of Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Search and rescue work continues, in hopes that living people may still be surviving in the tunnels of the region’s hydropower projects.

Yet Dr Samir Adhikari, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Health, told VaccinesWork that the government was alert to the need to prevent the spread of infectious disease in the flood-affected areas from the earliest days of the disaster.

Water sources flowing toward the communities have been tested and rapidly decontaminated, he reports. Another focus has been halting the rapid growth of mosquito populations, in a bid to brake the spread of mosquito-vectored disease in the deluged zone. Extensive search-and-destroy vector management programmes have been conducted.

Similarly, the government has jumped to conduct mass vaccination in those hardest-hit areas. Dr Abhiyan Gautam, Chief of Child Health and Immunization Services said 21,000 and 80,000 doses of cholera vaccine have already been administered to the people of Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts respectively after the flood.

Apart from that, the government has said that all required medicines and health workers have been adequately deployed in the affected areas to address any sort of health-related issues. In meantime, public health experts already deployed to the field are closely monitoring the risk for any other potential disease outbreaks, says Gautam.

A 50-year-old Singaporean climber, Lau Wee Seng, has died at an altitude of about 6,000m on Mount Manaslu in Nepal.

Lau fell ill and lost his pulse on 17 September during his descent from Camp II during an acclimatisation rotation.

A scientific review has pointed to climate-related instability, not just bad geological luck, in the glacier collapse that unleashed devastating flooding across Nepal and Tibet.

Researchers from World Weather Attribution and Imperial College London said long-term warming likely weakened the mountain landscape before the fatal Aug. 26 failure.

Here's what to know

According to The Guardian, the researchers concluded that rising heat helped destabilize the section of Langtang Lirung that broke away — an overhanging expanse of glacier and rock measuring about 2,153,000 square feet (200,000 square meters).

More than 1,300 people were killed, over 5,000 were still missing by September 17, and downstream communities were hit with little warning when a huge surge of water, ice, rock, and sediment tore through them.

Their analysis pointed to rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, thawing ground at high elevations, and possibly lingering effects from the region's 2015 magnitude-7.8 earthquake.

It also found that July and August 2026 were the hottest ever recorded locally, and that temperatures in the days leading up to the collapse were 8 degrees Fahrenheit (5 degrees Celsius) above the 30-year average.

Dr. Ben Clarke, a researcher on extreme weather and climate at Imperial College London, said the "fingerprints of climate change" were visible in the long-term changes around the glacier before it failed.

More background

Events on this scale are highly uncommon, the study said, with estimates suggesting a rock avalanche this large occurs roughly once every 1,000 to 10,000 years.

The researchers also reported that the Himalayas' freezing line has been rising by about 328 feet (100 meters) per decade since the 1980s. As a result, ground that used to stay frozen is thawing for longer periods, raising the odds of instability on steep mountain terrain.

The flood destroyed homes, roads, bridges, and settlements, stranding survivors and severing access to essential services.

The disaster also highlighted how communities that have contributed little to global warming can still endure some of its deadliest effects.

Dr. Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, said: "Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away."

What's being done?

According to the report, Nepal has formally sought financial help from the UN loss and damage fund to recover from the flooding.

The fund is designed to help countries deal with irreversible climate damage, and applications such as Nepal's partly rely on demonstrating a link between a disaster and a shifting climate.

The country's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, also urged major polluters, including China and India, to "wake up" and share responsibility for the disaster, according to The Guardian.

The analysis stops short of saying warming alone caused the collapse, but it said hotter conditions gradually destabilized the glacier's surrounding geology.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of World Weather Attribution, said: "In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that's done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed."

Where can I learn more?

Worldwide ice loss because of rising temperatures is increasing the risk of glacier collapse.

• Scientists have warned that a lot of glacial damage cannot be undone by future cooling.

• Researchers have outlined the extent of unprecedented glacier melt rates due to a warming planet.

• In Antarctica, Thwaites Glacier could trigger catastrophic sea-level rise if its collapse accelerates.

• In Svalbard, ocean warming is driving retreat at Austfonna, Norway's largest glacier.

title: Nepal youths begin hunger strike at 4,900 metres over glacial lake risks - The Kathmandu Post

full_article:
Eleven youths from Samagaun in Chumnubri Rural Municipality-1 of Gorkha district began an indefinite hunger strike on Friday at 4,900 metres near the Manaslu base camp, demanding action to reduce climate-related risks and protect glacial lakes.

Led by Dhawa Norbu Lama, the youths said they would continue the hunger strike until their demands were addressed.

“We started the hunger strike today and will continue until our demands are met,” Lama said, adding that they had no personal interests behind the protest.

The youths announced the protest on September 13 after seeing the loss of lives and property caused by the Bhotekoshi flood in Rasuwa. Their eight-point demands include aerial monitoring and depth measurements of glacial lakes in the Manaslu region and Chum Valley, and assessment of the risk of glacial lake outburst floods.

They have also called for water-level monitoring systems and warning sirens in lakes and rivers, as well as joint Nepal-China monitoring of glacial lakes in Tibet that could threaten settlements on the Nepali side of the border.

According to the World Health Organization , the flooding damaged homes, markets, roads, bridges, customs facilities and hydropower infrastructure across the region, prompting the government to declare 15 municipalities disaster-affected areas.

Surya grew up in Dhading, one of the districts hit hardest as floodwaters moved downstream from Rasuwa. That local grounding mattered immediately: with roads and bridges washed out across the region — CARE reports 32 bridges and nearly 25 miles of road were swept away, including the entire route linking Nuwakot to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing — teams without existing relationships and terrain knowledge struggled to reach communities cut off by the damage.

Describing a trip into the affected areas to deliver medical aid, Surya told Direct Relief it took "six or seven hours of off-roading from mountain to mountain." The organisation went on to deliver requested medications to Trishuli Hospital in Nuwakot and brought counsellors into Rasuwa to provide psychological first aid to displaced people in holding centres.

The two organisations leaned on an existing healthcare network and community ties built over years, loading emergency supplies and heading directly into Rasuwa and Nuwakot to distribute aid and, just as importantly, to start mapping what long-term recovery would require once the immediate crisis passed.

Following the August 2026 floods, it became the first organisation to commit funding to One Heart Worldwide's emergency response. Find out more.

Direct Relief.
